Factorials

The factorial of a whole number n, written n!, is the product of all whole numbers from n down to 1. It counts the ways to arrange n different objects in a row, and it appears throughout combinatorics, probability and calculus (Taylor series). Factorials grow astonishingly fast: 10!=3 628 800, and 70! already exceeds 10100. This calculator gives exact values with every digit up to 40 000!, and scientific notation beyond that.

Try changing the input

Watch the trailing zeros: 24! ends in 4 zeros but 25! ends in 6, because 25 contributes two factors of 5.

Definition and related formulas

n!=n×(n−1)×⋯×2×1,0!=1,n!=n×(n−1)!
FormulaMeaning
⌊n5⌋+⌊n25⌋+⋯Number of trailing zeros of n! (Legendre's formula).
n!≈2πn(ne)nStirling's approximation, used for very large n.

Why is 0!=1? There is exactly one way to arrange no objects, and the rule n!=n×(n−1)! with n=1 gives 1=1×0!.

Worked example

Compute 6! and count its trailing zeros

Step 1 — Multiply

6!=6×5×4×3×2×1=720

Step 2 — Trailing zeros

⌊65⌋=1

720 indeed ends in one zero.

Domain and precision

  • n must be a whole number from 0 to 1,000,000,000. Factorials of negative numbers are undefined (the gamma function extends factorials to other real numbers, but that is outside this calculator).
  • Up to n=40 000 the result is exact, computed with arbitrary-size integers; all digits can be viewed and copied.
  • Above that, the value is given in scientific notation from Stirling's series; the digit count and trailing-zero count are still exact.
